result.summary: Hercules performs his ninth labour, fetching the belt of the Amazon queen Hippolyte, and kills her after Hera stirs up trouble. On the way home he rescues Hesione at Troy. His tenth labour takes him west to Erythia to drive off the cattle of Geryon, which he finally delivers to Eurystheus after many fights and mishaps.

scenes.title: The belt of Hippolyte ordered
scenes.summary: Eurystheus orders Hercules to fetch the belt of Ares from the Amazon queen. The Amazons and their customs are described.

scenes.title: Paros and the Bebryces
scenes.summary: Hercules kills the sons of Minos on Paros after two of his men are slain, then helps Lycus defeat the Bebryces.
scenes.stakes: Hercules risks war and losing his men among hostile peoples.

scenes.title: Death of Hippolyte
scenes.summary: Hippolyte promises the belt, but Hera stirs the Amazons to attack. Hercules suspects treachery, kills Hippolyte and takes the belt.
scenes.stakes: Hercules faces an Amazon cavalry attack and the loss of his mission.

scenes.title: Hesione and the sea monster
scenes.summary: Laomedon cheated Apollo and Poseidon, who sent plague and a monster. Hercules saves Hesione but is denied his reward and threatens war.
scenes.stakes: Hesione faces being devoured; Troy faces destruction.

scenes.title: Home with the belt
scenes.summary: Hercules kills Sarpedon, subdues Thasos, kills two wrestlers at Torone, and gives the belt to Eurystheus.

scenes.title: Geryon and his cattle
scenes.summary: Hercules is ordered to fetch Geryon's cattle from Erythia. Geryon, his herdsman and his dog are described.

scenes.title: Pillars and the Sun's goblet
scenes.summary: Hercules travels west, sets up pillars, receives the Sun's goblet, kills the dog, Eurytion and Geryon, and ships the cattle across.
scenes.stakes: Hercules faces Geryon and his guardians alone.

scenes.title: The bull and Eryx
scenes.summary: Hercules fights robbers in Liguria, loses a bull in Sicily, and wrestles and kills Eryx to recover it.
scenes.stakes: Hercules risks losing part of the herd and his life in wrestling.

scenes.title: Hera's gadfly and the Strymon
scenes.summary: Hera scatters the cows in Thrace. Hercules gathers most, ruins the Strymon, and delivers them to Eurystheus.
scenes.stakes: Hercules risks losing the herd and failing the labour.

notable_quotes.reason: Classic account of the Amazons' custom of removing the right breast.

analysis.text: Hercules' labours carry him to the edges of the known world, and his violence often follows suspicion, insult or divine meddling, especially by Hera.
The western journey, pillars and founding of place names reflect Greek explanations of geography and colonisation, such as Italy from the bull.

legacy.text: The Pillars of Hercules became a name for the Strait of Gibraltar, and the tale influenced the Spanish pillars emblem.

fun_facts.text: The Library's text includes the explanation that Italy was named from the Tyrrhenian word for bull, one of several ancient etymologies.

language_notes.text: "Enjoined" means commanded or imposed; Eurystheus sets each labour as an order Hercules must obey.
"Trammelled" means hampered or restricted, literally caught in a net.
"To wit" is an old legal phrase meaning "that is to say" and introduces the list of names.
"In the room of" means "in place of"; the envoys offer two men as replacements for the slain.
"Stripped her of" means took the belt from her, here after killing her.
"Wantonness" here means reckless insolence or arrogance; the gods test whether Laomedon respects them.
Pergamum was the citadel of Troy.
Ganymede was a Trojan prince carried off by Zeus to serve as cupbearer; the mares were compensation to his father, Laomedon's kin.
"Stipulated" means agreed upon beforehand, referring to the promised mares.
"Lewd" here suggests wicked or insolent conduct rather than only sexual behavior.
"Kine" is an archaic plural of cow, meaning cattle.
Gadira is the region of Gades (modern Cádiz) in southwestern Spain, beyond the Strait of Gibraltar, at the western edge of the known world.
The two pillars are the traditional Pillars of Hercules, flanking the Strait of Gibraltar, marking the limit of the Mediterranean world.
"Hardihood" means boldness or daring; the Sun admires Hercules' audacity in threatening him.
The story explains the name Italy by a supposed local word "italus" for bull; this is an ancient folk etymology.
A gadfly is a biting insect that maddens cattle and drives them to scatter.

context_notes.text: Eurystheus, king of Mycenae, imposed the twelve labours on Hercules. This is the ninth.
Ares (the Greek war god) is said to have given the belt to Hippolyte as a mark of her rank among the Amazons.
Hera, queen of the gods, persecuted Hercules throughout his life, so she often interferes in his labours.
Troy is the city where Hercules' next adventure takes place, before the Trojan War.
Apollo was a god of plague and healing; Poseidon ruled the sea, so each sends a punishment fitting his domain.
Aenus was a coastal city in Thrace, on the northern Aegean.
The belt is that of Hippolyte, the Amazon queen, fetched as one of Hercules' labours for Eurystheus.
Typhon was a monstrous giant and Echidna a half-woman, half-serpent; their offspring include many fearsome creatures, such as Orthus.
Hades is the god of the dead; his cattle grazing in the west fit the region's association with the underworld.
Hera, wife of Zeus, persecutes Hercules throughout his life because he is her husband's son by another woman.
Eurystheus, king of Tiryns and Mycenae, imposed the twelve labours; sacrificing the cattle to Hera further mocks Hercules' efforts.

literary_notes.text: The Amazons' custom of removing a breast shows them as a society that puts war above conventional ideas of womanhood.
Hera's false rumour turns a peaceful agreement into violence; the promised gift is lost through deceit.
Hercules' sudden suspicion and killing of Hippolyte, though she had promised the belt, shows how Hera's trick succeeds.
Gods disguised as laborers build the city's walls, and the king cheats them, unaware of who they are; his impiety invites disaster.
A royal daughter exposed to a sea monster recalls the recurring myth pattern of sacrifice and rescue by a hero.
Hercules' threat of war on Troy anticipates his later sack of the city.
The vivid picture of a body joined at the waist and parted into three below stresses Geryon's monstrous, unnatural form.
Hercules' defiant bow aimed at the Sun shows his boldness and pride, which the god rewards rather than punishes.
Hera's hostile interference recurs across the labours, adding obstacles after Hercules seems to have succeeded.
